title: Variables (var, let, const)
summary: **Variables** are named containers for values. JavaScript declares them with `var`, `let`, or `const`, which differ in scope, whether they can be reassigned or redeclared, and how they behave before initialization (hoisting and the temporal dead zone).

subtopics.title: Declaration vs. assignment
subtopics.explanation: Declaring a variable creates the name; assigning gives it a value. With let and var you can declare now and assign later, while const requires assignment at declaration. Understanding the two steps explains why an un-assigned let is undefined and why const can't be left empty.

subtopics.title: Block scope vs. function scope
subtopics.explanation: let and const are block-scoped: they exist only inside the nearest { } block (an if, for, or any braces). var is function-scoped: it ignores blocks and lives in the whole enclosing function (or globally). Block scoping is more predictable and is the main reason to prefer let/const over var.

subtopics.title: Reassignment vs. redeclaration
subtopics.explanation: Reassignment changes the value of an existing variable; redeclaration declares the same name again. let allows reassignment but not redeclaration in the same scope; const allows neither; var allows both, which can mask bugs by silently overwriting an earlier variable.

subtopics.title: Hoisting and the temporal dead zone (TDZ)
subtopics.explanation: All declarations are 'hoisted' — the engine knows about them before the line runs. var is hoisted and initialized to undefined, so using it early gives undefined. let and const are hoisted but NOT initialized; using them before their declaration line throws a ReferenceError. That gap between the top of the scope and the declaration is the temporal dead zone.

subtopics.title: const with objects and arrays
subtopics.explanation: const prevents reassigning the variable, not mutating the value it points to. With objects and arrays, you can still add, change, or remove properties and elements because the binding stays the same — only the contents change. To truly freeze contents, use Object.freeze.

subtopics.title: Naming rules and conventions
subtopics.explanation: Variable names can contain letters, digits, $ and _, but can't start with a digit and can't be reserved words. By convention, JavaScript uses camelCase for variables and functions, UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for true constants, and descriptive names that say what the value represents. Good names make code self-documenting.
subtopics.example:
let firstName = 'Ada';      // camelCase
const MAX_RETRIES = 3;       // constant convention
let _private = true;         // leading underscore allowed

subtopics.title: Choosing between var, let, and const
subtopics.explanation: Modern guidance: default to const for values that don't get reassigned, use let when you need to reassign, and avoid var in new code. const signals intent (this won't change) and prevents accidental reassignment, while block scoping avoids the leakage and hoisting surprises var causes.

foundations.overview: A variable is a named reference to a value stored in memory. JavaScript gives you three ways to declare one — var (the original, function-scoped), and let and const (introduced in ES6, block-scoped). They differ in scope, mutability, redeclaration rules, and pre-initialization behavior. Choosing the right one makes code clearer and prevents a whole category of bugs.
foundations.formalDefinition: A variable declaration binds an identifier to a storage location within a scope. var creates a function-scoped (or global) binding that is hoisted and initialized to undefined; let creates a block-scoped, reassignable binding subject to a temporal dead zone; const creates a block-scoped binding that must be initialized and cannot be reassigned.
foundations.whyItMatters: Almost every line of JavaScript reads or writes a variable, so understanding scope and mutability is foundational. The differences between var, let, and const explain common bugs (leaked loop variables, accidental redeclaration, use-before-declaration) and underpin clean, predictable code.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a variable as a labeled box. let is a box whose contents you can swap out; const is a box you seal after putting something in (you can't swap the box, but if it holds a basket you can still rearrange the basket); var is an older box that ignores room dividers and can be relabeled at will.
foundations.browserPerspective: When the engine enters a scope, it creates the variable bindings up front (hoisting). var bindings are immediately set to undefined; let/const bindings are created but left uninitialized until execution reaches their declaration, enforcing the temporal dead zone. The engine resolves each variable reference against this scope structure.
foundations.realWorldUsage: const for imported modules, configuration values, and references you won't reassign; let for loop counters and accumulators; var almost never in modern code. Linters and style guides (Airbnb, StandardJS) enforce 'prefer-const' and 'no-var'.
foundations.businessImpact: Predictable variable behavior reduces bugs that reach production, lowering maintenance cost. Clear naming and const-by-default make codebases easier for new hires to read and safely modify.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Knowing scope and the TDZ prevents subtle bugs like the var-in-a-loop closure problem and use-before-declaration errors. Defaulting to const documents intent and lets tools catch accidental reassignment.
foundations.performanceImpact: The choice rarely affects raw performance, but block scoping can help engines and developers reason about variable lifetimes, and const signals immutability that can aid readability and refactoring safety more than speed.
commonUseCases: Declaring values that never change with const (config, references)
Loop counters and accumulators with let
Holding intermediate results in a calculation
Naming function results to make code self-documenting

commonMisconceptions.myth: const makes the value completely immutable.
commonMisconceptions.reality: const only prevents reassigning the variable; objects and arrays it points to can still be mutated. Use Object.freeze for deep immutability.

commonMisconceptions.myth: let and const are not hoisted.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They are hoisted, but not initialized — using them before their declaration throws a ReferenceError due to the temporal dead zone.

commonMisconceptions.myth: var, let, and const are interchangeable.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They differ in scope, reassignment, redeclaration, and hoisting behavior; using var can introduce bugs that let/const prevent.

visualExplorer.title: var vs. let vs. const through a scope
visualExplorer.caption: Step through how each keyword behaves as the engine enters a block and runs the code.

config.intro: Watch how declaration, hoisting, scope, and reassignment differ across var, let, and const.

steps.name: Enter the scope
steps.detail: The engine hoists all declarations: var is set to undefined, let/const are created but uninitialized (TDZ begins).

steps.name: Use before declaration
steps.detail: Reading a var gives undefined; reading a let/const throws a ReferenceError while in the TDZ.

steps.name: Reach the declaration line
steps.detail: let/const become initialized; const must be given a value right here.

steps.name: Reassign
steps.detail: var and let can be reassigned; const throws a TypeError if you try.

steps.name: Mutate an object
steps.detail: Even a const object can have its properties changed — const locks the binding, not the contents.

steps.name: Leave a block
steps.detail: let/const declared inside the block disappear; a var leaks out to the surrounding function.

interactiveExamples.title: let can change, const cannot
interactiveExamples.explanation: A let variable can be reassigned to a new value; attempting to reassign a const throws a TypeError. This is why we wrap the const reassignment in a try/catch to show the error.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: score: 20, then an Error about assignment to constant variable.

interactiveExamples.title: Block scope vs. function scope
interactiveExamples.explanation: var leaks out of the block it was declared in, while let stays contained. Reading the let outside its block throws a ReferenceError.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: I escaped, then an Error that trapped is not defined.

interactiveExamples.title: const objects are still mutable
interactiveExamples.explanation: You can change the properties of a const object because const only locks the binding. Reassigning the whole object, however, throws.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: The updated user object, then an Error about assignment to constant variable.

codeLab.title: Refactor var to const/let
codeLab.instructions: The starter uses var for everything. Refactor so values that never change use const and the accumulator uses let. Keep the output the same: the sum of the prices.
hints: Use const for the array since the binding never changes.
Use let for the accumulator and the loop counter because they are reassigned.

debuggingLab.title: Temporal dead zone surprise
debuggingLab.symptom: The code throws 'Cannot access count before initialization' instead of logging undefined.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: let declarations are hoisted but not initialized. Between the top of the scope and the declaration line, the variable is in the temporal dead zone, so reading it throws a ReferenceError. This differs from var, which would log undefined instead.
commonMistakes: Assuming let behaves like var and yields undefined when read early.
Believing let is not hoisted at all.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Move the access after the declaration so the variable is initialized before it is read.

theory.question: What is the difference between var, let, and const?
theory.directAnswer: var is function-scoped, hoisted and initialized to undefined, and can be redeclared and reassigned. let is block-scoped, hoisted but uninitialized (temporal dead zone), and can be reassigned but not redeclared in the same scope. const is also block-scoped with a TDZ, must be initialized at declaration, and cannot be reassigned. Modern code defaults to const, uses let when reassignment is needed, and avoids var.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Three keywords for declaring variables that differ in scope, mutability, redeclaration, and hoisting behavior.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: let and const were added in ES6 to fix var's confusing function scoping and hoisting, giving safer, more predictable block-scoped bindings.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: On entering a scope, var bindings are created and set to undefined; let/const bindings are created but stay uninitialized until their declaration line, enforcing the TDZ. const additionally rejects reassignment.

theory.whyImportant: It's one of the most common JavaScript interview questions and directly affects scope-related bugs and code clarity in everyday work.
theory.realWorldExample: Using let instead of var as a loop counter avoids the classic closure bug where all callbacks share one variable.

nestedTopics.title: Block vs. function scope
nestedTopics.explanation: let/const live in the nearest block; var lives in the whole function.

nestedTopics.title: Temporal dead zone
nestedTopics.explanation: let/const can't be read before their declaration line.

nestedTopics.title: Reassignment rules
nestedTopics.explanation: const can't be reassigned; let can; var can be reassigned and redeclared.

followUps.question: Why prefer const by default?
followUps.answer: It signals the binding won't change, prevents accidental reassignment, and makes code easier to reason about; use let only when you must reassign.

followUps.question: Can you redeclare a let in the same scope?
followUps.answer: No — that throws a SyntaxError; var allows redeclaration, which can silently hide bugs.

theory.question: Does const make a value immutable?
theory.directAnswer: No. const only makes the binding immutable — you cannot reassign the variable to a different value. If a const holds an object or array, you can still mutate its contents (change properties, push elements). For true immutability of the contents you need Object.freeze, and for deep immutability you must freeze recursively.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A clarification that const protects the variable binding, not the data it references.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Variables store either primitive values or references; const locks the reference, while the referenced object remains mutable by default.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Reassigning a const throws a TypeError, but operations like obj.prop = x or arr.push(x) change the existing object the const points to, which is allowed.

theory.whyImportant: Misunderstanding this leads to surprise mutations and a false sense of safety; it's a frequent interview follow-up.
theory.realWorldExample: A const config object can have its properties updated at runtime even though you can't replace the whole object reference.

nestedTopics.title: Binding vs. value
nestedTopics.explanation: const freezes the binding, not the underlying object.

nestedTopics.title: Object.freeze
nestedTopics.explanation: Prevents shallow changes to an object's own properties.

nestedTopics.title: Deep immutability
nestedTopics.explanation: Requires freezing nested objects too, or using immutable libraries.

followUps.question: How do you make a const object truly read-only (shallowly)?
followUps.answer: Use Object.freeze(obj); attempts to change its own properties then silently fail (or throw in strict mode).

scenario.question: A code review flags that a colleague used var throughout a new module. What concerns would you raise and what would you suggest?
scenario.directAnswer: I'd point out that var is function-scoped and hoisted, which leaks variables out of blocks, allows accidental redeclaration that hides bugs, and causes the classic loop-closure problem. I'd suggest defaulting to const for values that don't change and let where reassignment is needed, so the code is block-scoped and intentions are explicit, and I'd add an eslint 'no-var' / 'prefer-const' rule to enforce it.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A review situation about replacing var with block-scoped declarations.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: var predates ES6 and has scoping/hoisting quirks that modern keywords fix.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Switching to let/const adds block scoping and the TDZ, eliminating leakage and use-before-declaration surprises.

scenario.whyImportant: Choosing the right declaration prevents real bugs and improves maintainability across a team.

nestedTopics.title: Loop closure bug
nestedTopics.explanation: var in a loop shares one binding across callbacks; let gives each iteration its own.

nestedTopics.title: Linter enforcement
nestedTopics.explanation: Rules like no-var and prefer-const automate consistency.

followUps.question: Is there ever a reason to still use var?
followUps.answer: Rarely — mostly legacy code or very specific hoisting tricks; new code should prefer const/let.

coding.question: What does this loop log with var, and how would you fix it to log 0, 1, 2?
coding.thoughtProcess: var is function-scoped, so all the setTimeout callbacks close over the same single i. By the time they run, the loop has finished and i is 3, so it logs 3 three times. Switching the loop variable to let gives each iteration its own block-scoped binding, fixing the output.
coding.lineByLine: With var, there is one i shared by all three callbacks; after the loop it equals 3, so every callback logs 3. With let, each loop iteration creates a fresh, block-scoped i, so each callback captures its own value (0, 1, 2).

alternativeApproaches.title: IIFE capture with var
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Wrap the body in an immediately-invoked function that takes i as an argument, freezing its current value.
alternativeApproaches.code: for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) { ((j) => setTimeout(() => console.log(j), 10))(i); }

followUps.question: Why does let fix it without any other change?
followUps.answer: Each iteration gets a new, separately scoped binding of i, so each callback closes over its own value rather than a shared one.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Consistent variable declaration conventions (const-by-default, let-when-needed, no var) form part of a codebase's foundation, making scope explicit and refactors safer. Module-level const bindings document fixed dependencies and configuration.
productionDeepDive.performance: The keyword choice rarely affects runtime speed, but block scoping helps engines and developers reason about variable lifetimes; the bigger wins are correctness and readability rather than raw performance.
productionDeepDive.security: Avoiding accidental global variables (which var or undeclared assignments can create) reduces the risk of name collisions and unintended exposure of state on the global object.
productionDeepDive.scaling: As codebases grow, predictable block scoping and clear naming reduce cognitive load and merge conflicts, helping large teams modify shared code safely.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Defaulting to const communicates intent (this won't change), making code self-documenting; linters enforce prefer-const and no-var so the convention holds across contributors.
productionDeepDive.observability: Use-before-declaration and reassignment bugs surface as ReferenceError/TypeError at runtime; clear naming and stack traces, plus linters that catch many issues before runtime, aid debugging.

caseStudies.problem: Inconsistent var usage caused scope bugs and unreadable code across large teams.
caseStudies.solution: Mandated const-by-default with let only when needed and banned var via ESLint rules.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Minor friction adopting the rule vs. far fewer scope-related bugs.
caseStudies.lessons: Simple, enforced declaration conventions noticeably improve code quality at scale.

When would you choose let over const in this tracker?

keyTakeaways: var is function-scoped and hoisted to undefined; let and const are block-scoped and subject to the temporal dead zone.
let can be reassigned but not redeclared in the same scope; const cannot be reassigned and must be initialized at declaration.
const locks the binding, not the value — objects and arrays it points to can still be mutated.
Default to const, use let only when you must reassign, and avoid var in new code to prevent scope and hoisting bugs.
Use clear, conventional names (camelCase, UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for constants) so code reads as self-documenting.
